Common Name: VENUS'-HAIR FERN; SOUTHERN MAIDENHAIR; COMMON MAIDENHAIR

Plant Notes: As the only member of the genus in the USA, its nearest relatives are likely species in Mexico (Judd 1984).
This taxon can be treated at the specific rank as Andropogon hirsutior (Weakley et al. 2011).

An alternate taxonomy regards plants with stronger pubescence around the base of the blade as A. beyrichiana, restricted to SC, GA, AL, MS, and FL, and plants with stronger pubescence on the abaxial portion of the blade as A. stricta s.str, restricted to NC and SC (Peet 1993; Ward 2001). Other work favors treating both entities as one species (Walters et al. 1994; Kesler et al. 2003).
This species belongs in Aronia, which is only distantly related to Photinia (Guo et al. 2011; Li et al. 2012; Lo et al. 2012).

Arundinaria tecta is here provisionally included within A. gigantea (Radford et al. 1968; Godfrey 1988). Arundinaria tecta is characterized by a shorter height (usually < 2.5 m), air canals in the rhizome, 2-4 compressed basal internodes on primary branches, and terete internodes, while A. gigantea s.s. may be taller (usually > 2m, to 10 m) with rhizomes without air canals, 0-1 compressed internodes on primary branches, and internodes sulcate proximally (Triplett et al. 2006). The AFLP study by Triplett et al. (2010) showed that A. tecta from Atlantic coastal populations in GA, NC, SC, and VA is distinct from Appalachian and Gulf coastal populations of A. gigantea. In that study only a few populations of A. gigantea from the Florida panhandle were included, while no samples from peninsular Florida were included. Hall (2018) indicated A. gigantea was restricted to the panhandle in Florida, while A. tecta occurred in the central peninsula.
This species is now commonly placed in the genus Sceptridium.

Bulbostylis ciliatifolia var. coartcata (or B. coarctata) is considered a perennial (to annual in the north), which Kral (1971) "found it impossible to consider both [ciliatifolia and coarctata] as the same entity, but at the same time cannot avoid realizing the morphological closeness of the two". Other diagnostic characters for B. ciliatifolia var. coarctata include an inflorescence usually compound and of many, oblong or lance-linear spikelets with the longest bract of the inflorescence longer than the inflorescence, and edges of leaves usually distinctly tuberculate-scabrid.
Clinopodium is sometimes used as a temporary placeholder genus for this species. Although this species clearly does not belong in Clinopodium, its proper generic classification remains unresolved.

Clinopodium is sometimes used as a temporary placeholder genus for this species. Although this species clearly does not belong in Clinopodium, its proper generic classification remains unresolved. The disjunct populations of the peninsula may have larger corollas and have been referred to as Clinopodium macrocalyx (Shinners 1962).
A monograph of the genus did not cite any wild populations of this species in Florida (Barboza et al. 2022), cause for speculation that it is misapplied or introduced in Florida.

This species concept encompasses plants now referred to C. occulta (C. flexuosa, misapplied). Differentiating C. occulta and C. pensylvanica is challenging (Slenker et al. 2018; Hrusevar et al. 2021).

The domestication of the papaya probably began in southern Mexico and Central America (Carvalho & Renner 2012). This species is considered native to the state, as seeds of papaya dated to around the year 300 AD were found in Lee Co. (Ward 2011). Papapya is widely cultivated in Florida and certainly has escaped and naturalized from some of the cultivated strains. Small-fruited specimens of coastal and southern Florida (e.g. Franck 2615, Judd 5970) may represent native forms (Ward 2011).
This species can be placed in the genus Trilisa. The pleasant aroma of its leaves likened its use as an additive to tobacco (Rafinesque 1833; Wood 1881; Anonymous 1899; Karlsson 1972).
The suffix "trema" is to be treated as neuter (Nicolson 1994), necessitating the use of the epithet "americanum".
The suffix "trema" is to be treated as neuter (Nicolson 1994), necessitating the use of the epithet "floridanum".

The segregate known as C. ovalis or C. glabra var. odorata is sometimes recognized but apparently does not reach Florida (Little 1979). For the northern USA, Manning (1950: 191) wrote that he was unable to distinguish C. ovalis until "with completely mature fruit collected in November." Little (1979: 73) wrote that there were many trees with intermediate fruits and that the distributions of the two [C. glabra and C. ovalis] are nearly the same.

Common Name: PINELAND BUTTERFLY PEA; SAND BUTTERFLY PEA

Plant Notes: This species has been placed in the monospecific genus Fassettia (Mavrodiev et al. 2021).

Sometimes treated as an infraspecific taxon of C. laxum (Clark 1990; Wipff & Jones 1994), observations by Yates (1966) suggest C. laxum and C. sessiliflorum are not interfertile despite commonly being sympatric.
This taxon has sometimes been treated as a subspecies of Cladium mariscus. Verloove (2012) distinguished C. jamaicensis and C. mariscus primarily by their achenes.

This species probably needs to be accommodated in a different genus as it does not appear to be congeneric with Clinopodium vulgare, the type species of Clinopodium, nor with Micromeria juliana, the type species of Micromeria (Bräuchler et al. 2010).
In the closely related species, C. texanus, serotonin was characterized in the stinging hairs (Lookadoo & Pollard 1991) but was reportedly absent in C. stimulosus (Willis 1969).
The presence of scaly rhizomes is diagnostic for this species.
Though apparently only confirmed as present in Florida so far, this taxon is thought to be an introduction from the Old World (Faden 1993; Hassemer 2018).

According to Edwards et al. (2009), only the nutlet size clearly separates this taxon from C. canescens. All other morphological characters overlap. Conradina brevifolia is characterized as leaves 6-10 mm long and mature nutlets 1-1.25 x 0.5-9 mm. Leaves to 13 mm long are sometimes observed (e.g. Brass 33444 and Gilbert s.n., 287697).

In Florida, this mycoheterotrophic species has been found to derive its nutrients primarily from the ectomycorrhizal fungi Russula cf. amoenolens and R. cf. pectinatoides. Similar populations in the western USA and Mexico utilize different fungi (Thelephoraceae) and may be treated as a different species (Freudenstein & Barrett 2014).

Phipps & Dvorsky (2008) argued the name C. michauxii cannot be clearly applied, while Ward (2009) accepted the name. Various other names have been applied to specimens currently here under C. michauxii, some examples include C. attrita, C. egens, C. inops, C. integra, C. lacrimata, C. lepida, C. meridiana, C. munda, C. rava, C. recurva, C. vicana, and C. visenda. Crataegus flava had long been misapplied to specimens of this ilk (Phipps 1988; Phipps & Dvorsky 2007).

Common Name: AVON PARK RATTLEBOX; AVON PARK HAREBELLS
FLORIDA TREE FERN; RED-HAIR COMB FERN

Plant Notes: This species (along with several others) has been moved to the genus Ctenodon (Cardoso et al. 2020).
This taxon is closely related to C. lundelliana and C. martinezii, taxa of Mexico and Central America (Castellanos-Morales et al. 2018).

According to Dorr (2014), the correct name for Kyllinga pumila within Cyperus is Cyperus hortensis. Dorr (2014) also considered the name Kyllinga viridiflora could have priority if found to be validly published. The name Cyperus densicaespitosus has also been considered the accepted name (Carter et al. 2016) as has C. tenuifolius (Delahoussaye & Thieret 1967).

Small-leaved forms have gone by the name C. parvifolia. According to Thomas (1960: 99-103), the two forms "intergrade completely in certain local populations, and there is evidence of considerable gene exchange throughout the area of overlap" (see also Godfrey & Wooten 1981; FNA, vol. 8). Thomas (1960: 103-104) also did not find C. arida to be distinct morphologically or by habitat. See also: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/19201688
Following Isely (1986, 1998), D. adenopoda is recognized at the species level as no intergradation with D. pinnata is known.
Isely (1998: 501, 521-522) used the terms "merge insensibly", "confluent", and "intergrades" to characterize the two varieties of D. pinnata. (var. pinnata and var. trifoliata).

The circumscription of Nectandra, Ocotea, and related genera has long been problematic. The neotropical genus Damburneya with ca. 20 species was recently molecularly and morphologically defined by its reticulate tertiary leaf venation, tepals adaxially with straight hairs often intergrading with crinkled papillae-like hairs, filaments usually pubescent and narrower than the anthers, anthers smooth to lightly papillose and rounded, truncate, or emarginate at the tip (Trofimov et al. 2016).
DNA data indicate Harrisella is part of the leafless genus Dendrophylax (Carlsward et al. 2003; Molgo et al. 2016).
It has been proposed that D. carolinensis and D. micrantha should be considered synonyms of the earlier species name D. repens (Delgado 2019).

Austin (2007) considered this species native to Florida, partly based on observations of this species by W. Bartram (Harper 1958: 201, fig. 15) and A. Michaux (1803; Taylor & Norman 2002: 77, 114) . This species is now placed in the genus Distimake, but was previously included in Merremia, a genus which has been redefined to include only ten species (Simões & Staples 2017).

This species had frequently been placed in the monotypic genus Websteria. DNA work places this species in Eleocharis; furthermore, the submersed, branched habit is not unique to E. confervoides and is found in other African species of Eleocharis (Hinchliff et al. 2010).

Because of morphological and geographical overlap, infraspecific taxa were not recognized by Daniel (2013). Plants with narrow leaf blades in southern Florida have sometimes been called var. angustifolia.

Epidendrum magnoliae was listed by Muhlenberg in a catalogue without any physical description, making this name invalidly published and unusable (see Hágsater 2000). Muhlenberg only provided an abbreviated description of the genus Epidendrum and added that E. magnoliae was from "Car." [Carolina] which is insufficient for valid publication.
The recognition of this taxon at the species level as Equisetum prealtum has been advocated (Christenhusz et al. 2019).
As a species, this taxon takes the name E. floridanum, and is disjunct from E. longifolium (Floden 2022).
The suffix "botrys" is masculine (McNeill et al. 2012: Art. 62.2a).

This species extends to the neotropics (Yang & Berry 2011), but was reported as a Florida endemic in FNA (vol. 12). Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.
Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.
Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.

Common Name: COASTAL DUNE SANDMAT; SAND DUNE SPURGE
Plant Notes: Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.
Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.
Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.
This species may be endemic or is nearly so, with only a handful of reports from Alabama and Texas.

Euthamia graminifolia is considered absent from Florida, and these populations now fall under the name E. hirtipes (glabrous to hirtellous leaves; widespread in Florida) and E. scabra (scabrous leaves; only in panhandle in Florida) (Szubryt et al. 2020).
The genus Frangula is characterized by pentamerous flowers and naked winter buds, compared to Rhamnus which usually has 4-merous flowers and scaly winter buds  (Hauenschild et al. 2016).

Fraxinus profunda has been defined by its larger leaflets and samaras (Nesom 2010; Campbell 2017). The study by Whittemore et al. (2018) indicated F. profunda should be recognized as it is octoploid and consistently morphologically distinct from F. pennsylvanica (diploid).

Galactia floridana is characterized by its large flowers and villous stem vestiture. Two USF specimens collected from nearly the same time and place (Lakela 30270, 30273) show stem nodes which are near the main root putting down adventitious roots. As whole plants of Galactia with roots are rarely collected, it is uncertain if this is a unique or frequent habit of G. floridana (Nesom 2015, 2017).

This species is characterized by its strongly vining habit, stems usually obliquely retrorsely hispid to strigose, and relatively large flowers. This name had recently been misapplied to mostly prostrate plants (Ward & Hall 2004; Wunderlin & Hansen 2011), currently referred to here as G. purshii (Franck 2017).
Galium bermudense is now considered the earlier, accepted name for this species, with G. hispidulum being a later synonym (Reveal et al. 1987: 234).

Three entities can be recognized in the G. frondosa complex: G. frondosa s.str. (twigs glabrous to sparsely pubescent, leaf blades abaxially glabrous to sparsely pubescent, hairs 0.27-0.39 mm long, not glaucous to moderately glaucous, with golden yellow glands), G. nana (twigs pubescent, leaf blades abaxially glabrous to sparsely pubescent, hairs 0.13-0.26 mm long, usually strongly glaucous, with wide red glands), and G. tomentosa (twigs pubescent, leaf blades abaxially sparsely to densely pubescent, hairs 0.46-0.64 mm long, not glaucous, with golden yellow glands) (Godfrey 1988; Luteyn et al. 1996; Gajdeczka et al. 2010; Weakley et al. 2017). Monophyly of G. nana based on 40 ITS sequences of the G. frondosa complex was supported by 56% bootstrap support and a SNP (Gajdeczka et al. 2010). Six hybrids between G. nana and G. tomentosa and one hybrid of G. frondosa s.str. and G. nana were also supported by ITS sequences and morphology (Gajdeczka et al. 2010). Gaylussacia nana and G. tomentosa are generally sympatric in Florida, while G. frondosa s.str. is reported from the panhandle (e.g. R.R. Smith 1563 [FLAS], Orzell & Bridges 13034 [USF]).

Habenaria macroceratitis (ventral segment of petals more than twice the length of the dorsal segment; spur terete; of hardwood hammocks) is sometimes recognized as a distinct species (Brown 2000; Batista et al. 2011). Many authors have concluded the differences are confluent and H. macroceratitis should be considered a synonym of H. quinqueseta (Ackerman 2014). A DNA phylogeny found the two entities formed a monophyletic clade (Batista et al. 2013). A range-wide study is needed to determine if H. macroceratitis is an ecotype or a distinct species. Cocytius antaeus was found to visit their flowers (Stewart et al. 2007).
Though often placed in Echinodorus, this species is now typically placed in Helanthium (Chen et al. 2012; Ross et al. 2015; Trias-Blasi et al. 2015; Lehtonen 2017).

Often included in Diodia, this species belongs in the genus Hexasepalum, which is closely related to Ernodea and clearly removed from Diodia s.str. (Kirkbride & Delprete 2015; Salas et al. 2015; Cabaña Fader et al. 2016; Florentin et al. 2017). The genus Diodella had sometimes also been used.

This species was previously recognized in the genus Decumaria. Given the polyphyly of previous concepts of Hydrangea s.str., it appears best to merge several genera (incl. Decumaria) into an expanded Hydrangea s.lat. (De Smet et al. 2015).
Once placed in Panicum, the species is now placed with Hymenachne (tribe Paspaleae) and clearly does not belong in Panicum s.str. (Acosta et al. 2014, 2019).

This species is native and commonly cultivated. Distinctive features include the 7-15 flowers per inflorescence, greenish filaments, and orange pollen. A neotropical species not yet reported for Florida, Hymenocallis littoralis, is common in cultivation outside of Florida; this species has narrower leaves (2-3.8 cm wide) and 4-8 ovules per locule. Comparatively, H. latifolia has leaves 4-10 cm wide and 2 ovules per locule (Sealy 1954; Smith & Garland 2003).

Hypericum limosum, described from Cuba, was tentatively placed as a synonym of H. brachyphyllum (Adams 1962: 27-31). For a discussion of its application, see: https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2349860#page/20/mode/1up and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/19811114.

Common Name: HIGHLANDS SCRUB ST.JOHN'S-WORT; HIGHLANDS SCRUB HYPERICUM
ARCADIAN ST.JOHN'S-WORT; EDISON'S ST.JOHN'S-WORT; EDISON ASCYRUM
CREEPING BRAMBLE FERN; BARRINGTON'S BRAMBLE FERN
Plant Notes: Based on morphology, Florida material was recently described as a Florida endemic, Hypolepis barringtonii, which is a generally smaller plant with fewer prickles than H. repens s.str. (Schwartsburd 2018).
Plants with smaller leaves may represent a distinct species, referable as Ilex curtissii (Clark 2023).

Ilex arenicola was published in an August issue in 1924, while I. cumulicola was published in a September issue of the same year. Based on ITS sequence data, Germain-Aubrey et al. (2014) found support for a clade of I. cassine (incl. var. myrtifolia) sister to a clade of I. opaca (incl. var. arenicola). In another study, a specimen identified as I. cumulicola (provenance given as USA, voucher probably at G) was sister to a sample of I. rubra based on nuclear data, and sister to a sample of I. cassine based on plastid data (Manen et al. 2010).

Historically, this species was referred to as "cassina" (Alston & Schultes 1951) but then Linnaeus used that name for a different species, I. cassine (Schultes 1950; Edwin 1963). Although traditional usage  of this caffeine-containing plant (i.e. black drink) may have involved emesis (Merrill 1979; Crown et al. 2012), other studies indicate its potential for making a pleasant beverage (Wainwright & Putz 2014).

This species is considered endemic to Florida. The name is sometimes applied to plants in Hispaniola. Duncan & Duncan (1988) reported this species in Georgia from "a cultivated plant taken from the wild in Liberty Co." Darby (1841: 10) also reported it for the "lower districts of" Georgia.

Wood et al. (2020) reported one specimen each from Florida for I. coccinea (Buckley s.n., K) and I. hederifolia (Burkhalter 12850, UWFP). For I. coccinea (endemic to the SE USA), it is defined by its unlobed leaf blades, outer sepals 3 mm long with a 2-6 mm mucro (inner sepals 5 mm with a 2-5 mm mucro), and the pedicel becoming reflexed in fruit. For I. hederifolia (widespread in neotropics and SE USA), it has usually lobed leaf blades, the outer sepals 1.5-3 mm long (2-5 mm with mucro and inner sepals slightly larger), and the pedicel erect in fruit (Wood et al. 2020). O'Donell (1959) characterized I. hederifolia as having lobed or unlobed leaves, inner sepals to 3(-4) mm long, erect fruiting pedicels, and found from Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas south to northern Argentina, while I. coccinea had unlobed leaves, inner sepals 4-6 mm long, reflexed fruiting pedicels, and restricted from Georgia north to Rhode Island and west to Oklahoma (see also Wilson 1960; Wijnands 1983). Samples identified as I. coccinea from North Carolina and George were distinct from samples identified as I. hederifolia from Mexico and Papau New Guinea based on ITS sequences (Miller et al. 2004). The provenance of the earlier name I. coccinea (lectotype: LINN 219.3) was given as "Domingo" by Linnaeus, which allegedly (O'Donell 1959) actually referred to the type of I. hederifolia, Plumier's illustration, from Hispaniola.

This species seems best identified by its glabrous sepals (Felger et al. 2012), in comparison to the similar species I. cordatotriloba, I. lacunosa, and I. triloba. This species had been thought to originate from a cross between I. cordatotriloba and I. lacunosa. However, Duncan & Rausher (2013) found that I. leucantha was not interfertile with I. lacunosa. It is widespread and fecund (Felger et al. 2012) necessitating its recognition as a species (Duncan & Rausher 2013). Another genetically similar entity was given the provisional name Ipomoea austinii (non I. austinii Infante-Bet.), but was not formally described (Duncan & Rausher 2013).
This rather infrequent species is known only from the southeast USA where it is, of course, considered native (Austin & Huáman 1996). The flowers are nocturnal.

St. John (1970) treated this taxon at the species rank and characterized it as pantropical (absent from northern Indian Ocean) with leaf blades mostly longer than wide, unlobed or with lobe sinus less than 1/5 the length of the blade, lobes ascending, outer sepals 5-13 mm long, and cymes 1-20 flowered. Ipomoea pes-caprae subsp. pes-caprae is restricted to the northern Indian Ocean and has leaf blades wider than long, the lobe sinus 1/3-1/5 of the length of the blade, lobes divergent, outer sepals 7-12 mm long, and cymes 1-2 flowered. The two taxa apparently do not hybridize, or perhaps only rarely (Miryeganeh et al. 2014). Others chose to treat I. brasiliensis as a synonym of I. pes-caprae (Flora of China, vol. 16; Wood et al. 2020). This species apparently accumulates a relatively low amount of ergot alkaloids in its seeds (Amor-Prats & Harborne 1993), presumably via the endophytic ascomycete Periglandula.

Iris savannarum is common in Florida and is characterized by its bright green non-evergreen leaves, sepal tips more acute to acuminate, and capsules 6-10 cm long with 6 winglike ridges. The rarer plant, I. hexagona s.s., is characterized by its yellow-green and evergreen leaves, sepals tips less acute to rounded, and capsules 2.5-3.5 cm long and strongly hexagonal. Data from some microsatellites show that I. savannarum is composed of multiple lineages which likely can or do interbreed (Meerow et al. 2011, 2017). This and related species have been placed in the genus Phaeiris, and additional species have been recognized that occur in Florida, including albispiritus (extinct?), kimballiae, and rivularis (Mavrodiev et al. 2021).

Taxonomy in Juniperus is often very complex. If following Adams (1986; FNA vol. 2), the majority of Florida is represented by J. virginiana var. silicicola, distinguished by seed cones 3-4 mm, pollen cones 4-5 mm, bark cinnamon reddish, scale-like leaf apices bluntly obtuse to acute, and crown flattened. Juniperus virginiana var. virginiana occurs only in the extreme northern edge of Florida.

Populations in the Americas had been called K. virginica. Now the name K. pentacarpos is used since the American populations seem morphologically indistinguishable from the Eurasian populations (Blanchard 2008). Plants with narrower leaves (< 20 mm wide) with margins entire at the proximal half of the blade and reflexed lobes have been recognized as var. smilacifolia and endemic to peninsular Florida (Alexander et al. 2012), e.g. Jensen OS0563 (USF).
This species is thought to be endemic to only Highlands and Polk Cos., and was apparently reported in error for DeSoto Co. (Nesom in FNA, vol. 21).
Based on the trnk-matK plastid region, Lindernia dubia showed some molecular affinities with Micranthemum, not clearly resolved within Lindernia s.s. (Fischer et al. 2013).
This taxon was recently elevated to species rank (Bradley & Weakley in Weakley et al. 2020).
Sometimes placed as a variety of L. westianus, a phylogenetic study using RADseq data concluded that L. aridorum should be recognized at the species rank (Nevado et al. 2024; Bridges & Orzell 2024).

Recent studies concluded that L. diffusus should be emended to apply only to populations in the Florida panhandle and nearby states (Nevado et al. 2024; Bridges & Orzell 2024). Two related studies proposed alternative taxonomies: 1) L. cumulicola should be reinstated and its circumscription expanded to include all peninsular Florida populations along with recognition of infraspecific taxa (Nevado et al. 2024) or 2) recognize the peninsular Florida populations as four separate species (Bridges & Orzell 2024). (See also: Small 1933; Dunn 1971; Isely 1990; Duncan & McCartney 1992).
The oldest name for this species, Anagallis pumila, is blocked from being used in Lysimachia by a different species Lysimachia pumila Franch.

Here M. fluviatilis is treated as the only species in Florida and occurring throughout the American tropics. Carvalho (2007) retained M. aubletii as a synonym of M. fluviatilis, but based on subtle anther differences recognized M. kunthii and M. sellowiana as widespread species with rare occurrences in the southeastern USA. In a treatment focused on Cuba, Urquiola Cruz (2001) recognized M. aubletii and M. fluviatilis as distinct species, giving them virtually the same distribution as throughout the American tropics, and distinguished M. fluviatilis by being generally erect plants with leaves spirally arranged with short bifurcate apices, pedicels 1-5 mm or rarely to 10 mm long, petals white, pink, or purple and rounded at the apex, and capsules oblong-elliptic vs. M. aubletii as generally creeping plants with leaves arranged on the dorsal and lateral part of the stems and without bifurcate apices, pedicels 5-30 mm long, petals white to pink-purple and emarginate at the apex, and capsules subglobose to ovoid.

This achlorophyllous mycoheterotrophic species is mainly linked with ectomycorrhizal species of Russulaceae (Bidartondo & Bruns 2001; Kong et al. 2015). A recent study provides support for the recognition of M. brittonii, possibly endemic to Florida, with tapered filaments (apical width 0.55-0.85 times the basal width), larger petals, stamens, and ovaries, hairier petals and filaments, nectar spurs divergent (ca. 50-110 degree angle), largely confined to scrubby habitats, and mycorrhizal with species of the Lactifluus deceptivus complex (perhaps L. arcuatus, L. caeruleitinctus) (Keesling 2020).
As a species, this taxon would take the name M. sericea.

Common Name: CELESTIAL LILY; FALLFLOWERING IXIA; HAPPYHOUR FLOWER

Plant Notes: Listera is subsumed into Neottia (Barone Lumaga et al. 2014; Freudenstein & Chase 2015).
Nolina floridana McFarlin, nom. inval. (1935: 80) may be referable to this species.
Because of its divergent morphology from other species of Ophioglossum, this species has often been classified in Cheiroglossa (Shinohara et al. 2013; PPG I 2016).
The genus Pteroglossaspis has now been subsumed into Orthochilus (Martos et al. 2014; Bone et al. 2015).

The typical variety, var. regalis, is found in the Old Word (Fernald 1930). Treating the American taxon, var. spectabilis, as a distinct species has also been advocated based on analysis of DNA which suggests var. spectabilis is more closely related to O. japonica (Metzgar et al. 2008; Tsutsumi et al. 2011; Arana et al. 2015; Schneider et al. 2015).
This species was once known as Reimarochloa oligostachya, but the genus Reimarochloa has since been found to be part of Paspalum (Scataglini et al. 2014).

Within this group, some treatments recognize two species: P. pallida (hypanthium 2.8-4.1 mm wide, inner coronal filaments < 1.4 mm long), native to Florida, Texas, West Indies, Mexico, Central America, and Venezuela, and P. suberosa s.str. (hypanthium usually 4.0-8.8 mm wide, inner coronal filaments > 1.4 mm long) native to the West Indies, Mexico, Central and South America, with both introduced in the Old World tropics (Porter-Utley 2003, 2014). Based on an ITS phylogeny, a cultivated specimen (Porter-Utley P-65, FLAS) identified as P. pallida with provenance putatively from the Everglades fell within a strongly supported monophyletic clade of P. pallida + P. suberosa with pallida aff., while the specimen identified as "P. suberosa with pallida aff." was from Sarasota Co. (Abbott 14284, FLAS) and had four different ITS copies falling in multiple clades (Porter-Utley 2014). The use of P. suberosa s.lat. is similar to other treatments (Long & Lakela 1971; Adams 1972; Correll & Correll 1982; Proctor 1984; Bornstein in Howard 1989).

Common Name: COMB POLYPODY; SWAMP PLUME POLYPODY; PALMLEAF ROCKCAP FERN

Plant Notes: The species in Florida is sometimes recognized as P. glaber (Judziewicz & Guala 2007 in FNA, vol. 24), or P. glaber is sometimes placed as a synonym of P. lappulaceus (Judziewicz et al. 2000).

Freytag & Debouck (2002) wrote that "this taxon apparently has an overlapping range with the type species, yet it is very distinct and there seems to be no intergradation [...] On the other hand, the similarities are so great that the senior author sees no reason at this time to maintain the specific rank."

Common Name: SOUTHERN TUBERCLED ORCHID; PALEGREEN ORCHID; GYPSY-SPIKES

Plant Notes: It has been suggested that this species and Platanthera clavellata and P. integra belong in the genus Gymnadeniopsis (Brown 2002; see FNA, vol. 26).
This is presumably recently introduced in south-central Florida.

The appropriate name for this orchid may be problematic, partly because of the interpretation of Satyrium latifolium, which has been applied to three different species recently. As pointed out by Jarvis (2009: 96, 819), it is a legitimate name validated by reference to a description in Plantarum Jamaicensium Pugillus. Ackerman (2014) and Ormerod (2013, 2016) both mistakenly interpreted the name as invalid (nom. nud.). Jarvis (2009; Jarvis & Cribbs 2009) interpreted the type of S. latifolium (LINN 1055.6) to be Erythrodes hirtella, which may be a good match based on the size of the leaves (as given in Ackerman 2014). Ackerman (2014: 333, 366) interpreted LINN 1055.6 to be Microchilus plantagineus. Ormerod (2013, 2016) interpreted LINN 1055.6 to be Aspidogyne querceticola. The Linnaean name, S. latifolium, would have priority for whatever species it was applied to (although the specific epithet is blocked in Erythrodes by a different species, E. latifolia (Blume) Blume). Some studies prefer to use the genus Aspidogyne, considering Platythelys a generic synonym (Meneguzzo 2012; Ormerod 2013). POWO maps Microchilus querceticola as the species in Florida.

Though sometimes considered non-native, the available evidence of its pre-Columbian presence in the Americas (Gray & Trumbull 1883a, 1883b:138; Byrne & McAndrews 1975) favors its classification as native. Among leaves, it has one of the richest known sources of a-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid (Simopoulos & Salem 1986; Omara-Alwala et al. 1991; Simopoulos et al. 1992; Liu et al. 2000).

Pseudoziziphus contains two species, this one and P. parryi of the southwestern USA and northwestern Mexico. The genus Pseudoziziphus is related to Condalia, both of which are well separated from Ziziphus s.s. (Hauenschild et al. 2016).
According to Hunt (1991: 118), the leaves of Q. inopina have quercetin 3-O-diglucoside, which is never found in Q. myrtifolia.

Common Name: LAUREL OAK; DIAMOND OAK; DARLINGTON OAK
Plant Notes: This is a s.lat. species concept. Hunt (1991:74) characterized Q. hemisphaerica as leaves essentially evergreen, blades 3.5-5.5 x 0.7-1.6 cm, basal angle 94-244, apical angle 49-153, coriaceous, lustrous, often dentate, slightly revolute, opaque, essentially glabrous, venation more prominent adaxially, petiole 0.7-1.8 mm, twigs grayish vs. Q. laurifolia s.str. as leaves tardily deciduous, blades 6.5-8.8 x 1.8-2.6 cm, basal angle 20-130, apical angle 144-213, moderately coriaceous, moderately lustrous, never dentate, not revolute, translucent, venation more prominent abaxially, twigs reddish tinted. Hunt (1991:200) also wrote it was the "most difficult pair of taxa to assess"; "It is possible that widespread introgression occurs" and that leaves of Q. hemisphaerica from wet lowlands and of Q. laurifolia from dry uplands often resemble each other which is "particularly evident in Florida" where the two are "abundant yet highly variable" (1991:364); the two "cannot be distinguished chemically" (1991:119); and it "may not always be possible to identify individuals of these species from a single branch" and "it is often unreasonable to expect identification from a single leaf of these species" (1991:204). Monk (1965) summarized the occurrence of Q. laurifolia s.lat. in 60 communities of north peninsular Florida, reporting it as present in 85% of dry, 51% of dry-mesic, 35% of mesic, 49% of wet-mesic, and 31% of wet sites. Duncan & Duncan (1988) observed that Q. hemisphaerica flowered two weeks later in the same general area, also supported by Hunt (1991:164-165). In west-central Florida, flowering specimens of this group have been documented from Jan 28 (Perkins s.n., acc. no. 1966) through Mar 25 (Cole LR0114). The distribution of the two entities in the southeast USA is nearly identical, but Q. hemisphaerica is considered more common in xeric conditions and Q. laurifolia in more hydric conditions. Hipp et al. (2017) found samples of Q. hemisphaerica from North Carolina were more closely related to other species than to Q. laurifolia from Florida.

This species can be found in a variety of habitats, from lowlands to uplands. One of its synonyms is Quercus aquatica, named by Walter in 1788. The moniker "water oak" has been in use for a long time, but may be perceived as a misnomer since the species can commonly be found in well drained uplands. When cut, trunks may exude copious water, perhaps relating to the common name.
The use of Q. elliottii for this species is also common because of the incongruence of Walter's protologue of Q. pumila with this species (Wilbur & Ho 2008).

Rehder (1921) excluded R. viscosum from Florida and instead recognized R. serrulatum as the species in Florida. A comparison and discussion of the differences can be found here, pages 153-166: https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/67651#page/171/mode/1up.

Rhynchospora intermedia Beyrich ex Kunth was not validly published (Art. 36.1), which allows R. intermedia (Chapm.) Britton to be a valid and legitimate name. This makes R. pineticola an illegitimate name that is homotypic with R. intermedia. Curiously, Chapman's description of R. plumosa var. intermedia (basionym of R. intermedia) is very similar to R. marliniana.
This species was previously treated in a broader concept by Long (1964) to include R. ciliosa, R. heteromorpha, and R. succulenta, differing from the current taxonomy adopted here.
This taxon is best considered a distinct species, as it was not recovered as part of the S. graminea species clade based on a DNA phylogeny (Ito et al. 2020).
The allozyme studies by Hauber & Lege (1999) are intriguing with respect to the taxonomy of S. graminea. It was based mostly on samples from LA and MS and two samples from the FL panhandle.

Bicknell (1897) described S. floridana (later reduced to a variety by Wolff) as a commonly smaller plant with more numerous, closely spaced cauline leaves with fewer and larger teeth. Bicknell (1897) was also of the opinion that typical S. canadensis occurred in Florida. Shan & Constance (1951) stated that S. floridana "seems to have no distinct features deserving special status".
Usually classified as a member of Scirpus or Schoenoplectus, this species has now been moved into the genus Schoenoplectiella (Lye 2003; Glon et al. 2017).

Other entities are sometimes recognized in this group, such as S. flaccida, S. minor, and S. nitida. Scleria minor has been characterized by being smaller (leaves 1-2.5 mm wide and achenes 1.5-2 mm long) (Reznicek et al. in FNA, vol. 23). Kessler (1987) noted "that a series of variations occurs between S. triglomerata and S. minor" and S. flaccida and S. nitida "represent variations of S. triglomerata, and their classification as separate species can not be justified."

Species Author: (Michx.) J. F. B.Pastore & J. R. Abbott

Plant Notes: Included here as synonyms, S. littoralis and S. rubromarginata have been recognized as Florida endemics (Siedo 2014). Plants of the pine rocklands are generally low, spreading with several basal branches.
The taxon S. fuscatum was split from S. nashii in FNA (vol. 26) and stated to occur in Florida.

The earlier name Smilax tamnoides is sometimes preferred for this species (Fernald 1944; FNA, vol. 26), while S. hispida is commonly preferred (Clausen 1951; Wilbur 2003). The thorns depicted in the type illustration of S. tamnoides appear anomalous for this species: https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/126524#page/225/mode/1up
Recent work uses the name S. mexicana for Florida material and restricts S. sempervirens to North Carolina and northward (Semple et al. 2016).
As part of the genus Sporobolus, this taxon takes the name Sporobolus bakeri.
Spermacoce prostrata might be considered part of Spermacoce s.str. (Salas et al. 2015; Florentin et al. 2017).
Known only from Polk Co., this species effloresces Aug-Sep,  whereas the very similar S. longilabris does so Nov-Dec.
Recent work has provided evidence for treating S. eatonii as synonymous with S. lacera (Dueck et al. 2014; Pace 2015; Pace & Cameron 2016).

Common Name: FRAGRANT LADIESTRESSES; MARSH LADIESTRESSES; UNDERWATER ORCHID

Plant Notes: Recent work shows S. sylvatica is within the S. praecox lineage (Dueck et al. 2014; Pace 2015; Pace & Cameron 2016), suggesting it is an ecotype or could perhaps be treated as a subspecies (Pace 2015).

This species was recently reinstated and removed from its previous synonymy under S. cernua or S. odorata (Pace & Cameron 2016). Additionally, two names of alleged hybrids (S. x folsomii & S. x itchetuckneensis) have been subsumed into synonymy under S. triloba.

The Linnaean protologue of the basionym spelled the epithet as "polyrhiza" which is retained here, although Schleiden then changed the epithet to "polyrrhiza" when making the combination in Spirodela, a spelling used by some authors.
Sporobolus osceolensis was recently described, endemic to central and north peninsular Florida. Link here: https://www.phytoneuron.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/20PhytoN-Sporobolusosceolensis.pdf

This species was once considered endemic to Florida (Small 1933) and it may have recently spread into adjacent states. It is known from Georgia by at least 1945 (Hardy s.n., GA), Alabama by 1950 (Wilson & Orr s.n., TROY, UWAL), and South Carolina by 1956 (Freeman 56171, CM).

This grass is widely planted and various cultivars have been characterized (Busey 1995, 2003; Komma 2003). While the rest of the genus is native to the eastern hemisphere, this species is nearly pantropical and presumably native at least to Africa and the Americas (Sauer 1972). Sauer (1972) noted that the "species as a whole is primarily a coastal pioneer".

Common Name: SHOWY DAWNFLOWER; HIDDEN STYLISMA; AUSTIN'S DAWNFLOWER
Plant Notes: This species was probably first recognized by James B. McFarlin as Stylisma flagellaria, nom. inval. (McFarlin 1935: 168).
Recent taxonomies place this species in the genus Christella (Almeida et al. 2016; PPG 2016; Fawcett & Smith 2021).
Recent taxonomies place this species in the genus Cyclosorus (Almeida et al. 2016; PPG 2016).
This taxon is part of Thelypteris s.str. (Almeida et al. 2016; PPG 2016).
Recent taxonomies place this species in the genus Amauropelta (Alvarez-Fuentes 2010; Almeida et al. 2016; PPG 2016).

Common Name: TOOTHED LATTICE-VEIN FERN; DENTATE LATTICE-VEIN FERN
Plant Notes: Recent taxonomies place this species in the genus Meniscium (Fernandes et al. 2014; Almeida et al. 2016; PPG 2016).
A recent study recognized 10 species of Trichostema in Florida (McClelland 2022; McClelland et al. 2023; see also Lewis 1945; Huang et al. 2002).
This species can cause a stinging sensation (Coile 1999) probably due to injection of neurotransmitters and other irritants when handled.

Vaccinium corymbosum s.lat. and V. darrowii are two important species for blueberry production for human consumption in Florida (Lyrene 1997; Ehlenfeldt & Ballington 2012). Within V. corymbosum s.lat. and included here, Vaccinium elliottii is characterized by leaf blades less than 3.5 cm long (Godfrey 1988; Luteyn et al. 1990). Other taxa that may be recognized and occur in Florida are V. formosum, V. fuscatum, and V. virgatum (Ward 1974; Weakley 2015). Vaccinium corymbosum s.str., V. caesariense (reported by Camp 1945), and V. tenellum are not known from Florida (Ward 1974; Ward & Lyrene 2007).
This species has been hybridized with highbush blueberry to produce cultivars for production of blueberries (Chavez & Lyrene 2009).

Five varieties were recognized for Florida by Ward (1974): var. caesium (pedicels and twigs without stipitate glands, fruit glabrous, flowers solitary and scattered, subtended by leaves of normal size or somewhat smaller, many leaf blades abaxially whitened-glaucous), var. glandulosum (pedicels and twigs densely stipitate-glandular), var. multiflorum (pedicels and twigs without stipitate glands, fruit pubescent, calyx and hypanthium sparingly pubescent, lacking stipitate glands, flowers in axils of normal sized leaves), var. sericeum (pedicels and twigs without stipitate glands, fruit pubescent,  calyx and hypanthium densely hirsute, often with intermixed stipitate glands, flowers usually in axils of very reduced leaves), and var. stamineum (pedicels and twigs without stipitate glands, fruit glabrous,  flowers in distinct inflorescences or sprays, subtended by greatly reduced leaves, leaf blades abaxially green).
This species had previously been placed in the monotypic genus Stylodon. However, this species appears to be a part of Verbena (Marx et al. 2010; Nesom 2010).

Using RAD-seq data, V. nitidum was strongly supported as a distinct species and lineage apart from V. nudum (Spriggs et al. 2019). Based on morphology, species assignment may sometimes be "ambiguous" (Spriggs et al. 2019). Generally, V. nitidum has smaller leaves and shorter peduncles and appears to be quite common in northern Florida (panhandle to the peninsula, at least south to Alachua Co.). Kurz & Godfrey (1962) distinguished two species but based more on qualities of the vestiture, venation, albedo, and blade margins (their V. nudum had wider but not longer leaf blades). For V. nitidum, Aiton provided a very brief morphological description with vague provenance and apparently the name has not been typified.
According to Ballard et al. (2023), plants of the southeastern USA are V. vittata and V. lanceolata is generally allopatric in more northern parts of the USA.

A recent nuclear DNA phylogeny found that two samples from Florida (Sumter & Taylor Co.) referred to as V. rufotomentosa formed a clade sister to a Florida sample (Leon Co.) identified as V. aestivalis, together embedded in a broader V. aestivalis clade which further included another Floridian (Gadsden Co.) V. aestivalis (Talavera et al. 2023). A plastome analysis recovered two Florida samples tenatively called V. rufotomentosa to form a clade apart from other samples (from Texas and New Jersey) (Wen et al. 2018).

Reported for Florida are hybrids between W. bahamensis and W. indica and hybrids between W. bahamensis and W. glabra (FNA, vol. 6), although W. glabra is considered endemic to the West Indies and is not known from Florida (Acevedo-Rodríguez & M.T. Strong 2012).

Yucca flaccida has been recognized as a distinct species (Hess & Robbins, FNA, vol. 26; Ward 2006, 2011). A DNA phylogeny placed it (based on a cultivated specimen) as a member of the otherwise fleshy-fruited Aloifolia clade (Ayala-Hernández et al. 2025).

Two varieties of this species in Florida are recognized by Griffith et al. (2021) and five were recognized by Ward (2016). This taxonomy recognizes Z. integrifolia as native to Florida and the Bahamas, and Z. pumila as endemic to the West Indies (Stevenson 1987; Salas-Leiva et al. 2013; Ward 2016). Previous taxonomies had used Z. pumila to refer to plants in Florida (Eckenwalder 1980). The starchy subterranean stem has been used a food source (Clevenger 1921; Hann 1986; Austin 2004). The plant also contains the toxic azoxy glycoside cycasin (Castillo-Guevara & Rico-Gray   2003), and food from Zamia must be properly prepared to remove this toxin. The butterfly Eumaeus atala accumulates cycasin as it feeds on Zamia (Rothschild et al. 1986.) BMAA is a neurodegenerative toxic amino acid that is potentially found in this species (Schneider et al. 2002), probably produced by the plant and not cyanobacteria (Solonenka 2023).
